decks.domain: Defensive driving: night driving, driving situations, emergencies, vehicle failures and crashes

cards.front: How much of a driver's decision making depends on sight, and what happens to that vision after dark?
cards.back: Roughly ninety percent of the decisions a driver makes depend on what they can see, and that vision shrinks after dark.
cards.memory_hook: you decide by what you see

cards.front: At night, how should your speed relate to the reach of your headlights?
cards.back: At night, slow down and stay within the reach of your headlights so the vehicle can always stop inside the distance you can actually see.

cards.front: What does the manual's night stopping table assume, and how far does a vehicle travel each second at sixty miles per hour?
cards.back: The manual's night stopping table assumes low beams and a nighttime reaction time of one point five seconds, and notes that a vehicle covers eighty-eight feet each second at sixty miles per hour

cards.front: On low beams at twenty miles per hour, what reaction, braking and total stopping distances does the night table list?
cards.back: On low beams at twenty miles per hour, the table lists forty-four feet of reaction distance plus thirty-one feet of braking distance, for seventy-five feet of total stopping distance.

cards.front: On low beams at forty miles per hour, what reaction, braking and total stopping distances does the night table list?
cards.back: On low beams at forty miles per hour, the table lists eighty-eight feet of reaction distance plus one hundred twenty-three feet of braking distance, for two hundred eleven feet in total.

cards.front: On low beams at sixty miles per hour, what reaction, braking and total stopping distances does the night table list?
cards.back: On low beams at sixty miles per hour, the table lists one hundred thirty-two feet of reaction distance plus two hundred seventy-seven feet of braking distance, for four hundred nine feet in total.

cards.front: On low beams at seventy miles per hour, what reaction, braking and total stopping distances does the night table list?
cards.back: At seventy miles per hour on low beams at night, the table lists one hundred fifty-four feet of reaction distance plus three hundred seventy-six feet of braking distance, for five hundred thirty feet in total.

cards.front: Besides staying within headlight reach, what other rules does the manual give for night driving?
cards.back: Other night rules are to drive more slowly than in daylight, watch for road signs, slow or unlit vehicles, bicycles, pedestrians and animals, and keep wider safety margins.

cards.front: When do headlights belong on?
cards.back: Headlights belong on at dusk, at night, at dawn, on dark days, and any time weather cuts visibility to under five hundred feet.

cards.front: What does New Jersey law require whenever the windshield wipers are running?
cards.back: New Jersey law requires headlights to be on whenever the windshield wipers are running.

cards.front: Who has the right of way in a crosswalk, and must you stop if the crosswalk is not marked?
cards.back: In a crosswalk, pedestrians and people using wheelchairs or mobility-assistance vehicles always have the right of way, and drivers must stop for pedestrians whether or not the crosswalk is marked.

cards.front: How far ahead should you scan while driving?
cards.back: Scan at least twelve seconds ahead, meaning you should spot objects far enough away that reaching them would take at least twelve seconds.

cards.front: On a clear city street at twenty-five miles per hour, what does scanning far enough ahead work out to?
cards.back: On a clear city street at twenty-five miles per hour, looking that far ahead works out to seeing about one block in front of you.

cards.front: In heavy city traffic, how do you get the extra time you need to react?
cards.back: In heavy city traffic you need extra time to react, which means slowing down, since a lower speed buys time.

cards.front: How should you approach an intersection, and where should your vehicle be at its slowest?
cards.back: Approaching an intersection, slow down, glance left and then right, and keep your foot on the brake; at the crosswalk itself the vehicle should be at its slowest.

cards.front: What is true of an intersection with no lights or signs, and who must avoid a collision there?
cards.back: An intersection with no lights or signs has no traffic control at all, even if the road is wide, smooth or busy, so avoiding a collision there is entirely up to the driver.

cards.front: How common is speeding as a crash factor, and do highway crashes happen in good conditions?
cards.back: Going over the posted limit or too fast for conditions is among the most common factors in crashes, which happen on highways even in good weather on dry pavement.

cards.front: What danger do wide-open highways pose, and how should drivers respond?
cards.back: Wide-open highways can tempt drivers to relax, but some have no signals at crossroads, so drivers must stay alert, drive defensively and keep within the speed limit.

cards.front: What hazards do warning signs mark, and why should you slow down there?
cards.back: Warning signs mark hazards such as hills, dips, narrow bridges, bumps and railroad tracks; slow down there, because speeding and then braking hard can cause a skid or a spin.

cards.front: In farm country or open land, what should you do when an animal is in the road?
cards.back: In farm country or open land where livestock or deer may cross, slow down for an animal in the road until it has passed, since animals move unpredictably.

cards.front: What happens to motor vehicle fines in a New Jersey roadway construction zone?
cards.back: In New Jersey, fines for motor vehicle violations double when they are committed in a roadway construction zone.

cards.front: How far ahead of the work area can a work zone be announced, and by what?
cards.back: A work zone is announced as far as one-half mile ahead of the work area, either by an advance warning sign or by a vehicle with flashing lights.
cards.memory_hook: warned up to half a mile

cards.front: What two ways may drivers be routed around a work zone?
cards.back: Drivers may be routed around a work zone by a detour that uses a different road, or by a diversion such as a lane shift or a crossover through the median.

cards.front: What are the basic rules for driving through a work zone?
cards.back: Work zone basics are to stay fully attentive, obey signs and flaggers, turn on headlights so workers can see you, avoid tailgating and keep to the posted speed limit.

cards.front: What distractions should you avoid in a work zone, and what else should you do there?
cards.back: Through a work zone, avoid distractions such as changing radio stations or hands-free calls, watch for workers and equipment, and be patient with the crews.

cards.front: What marks the place where normal driving can resume after a work zone?
cards.back: An End Road Work sign, or the last temporary traffic control device, marks where normal driving can resume after a work zone.

cards.front: How many fatal and serious injury crashes do work zones see across the nation each year?
cards.back: Across the nation each year, work zones see nearly eight hundred fatal crashes and over 37,000 serious injury crashes.

cards.front: When does an ignition system let you remove the key?
cards.back: An ignition system lets you remove the key only when the transmission is in Park.

cards.front: Why must you never turn a steering-wheel ignition to lock while the vehicle is moving?
cards.back: Never turn a steering-wheel ignition to the lock position while the vehicle is moving, because the steering locks as the vehicle turns and you lose control.

cards.front: What usually causes skids, and does the drive type change how you handle them?
cards.back: Skids usually come from sudden turns, lane changes or hard braking, often on wet or icy roads, and are handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles.

cards.front: If the rear of the vehicle slides, what should you do with the gas, the wheel and your eyes?
cards.back: If the rear of the vehicle slides, lift your foot off the gas and steer in the direction the rear is skidding without oversteering, while looking where you want to go.

cards.front: What can happen if you turn the wheel sharply away from a skid, and should you brake in a side skid?
cards.back: Turning the wheel sharply away from the direction of a skid can make the vehicle spin, and during a side skid you should not use the brakes.

cards.front: What should you do once the vehicle feels back under control after a skid?
cards.back: Once you feel the vehicle is back under control after a skid, straighten the wheels.

cards.front: For an emergency stop, how do you leave a highway onto a paved shoulder, and onto an unpaved one?
cards.back: For an emergency stop on a highway with a paved shoulder, signal and move onto the shoulder at or near traffic speed before slowing; on an unpaved shoulder, slow to a safe speed before leaving the road.

cards.front: After stopping on the shoulder, where do you set the warning devices?
cards.back: After stopping on the shoulder, set a flare or warning sign just behind the vehicle and another warning device at least three hundred feet back, about one hundred twenty paces.

cards.front: Once on the shoulder, what lights, hood and signal steps does the manual list?
cards.back: Once pulled onto the shoulder, turn on parking or emergency lights, never stand where you block the taillights at night, raise the hood, and tie a white cloth to the antenna or left door handle if you need help.

cards.front: If the wheels drift onto the shoulder, how do you get back onto the pavement?
cards.back: If the wheels drift onto the shoulder, do not jerk back onto the pavement; stay on the shoulder, ease off the gas, and once at twenty-five miles per hour or less turn the wheel one-quarter turn toward the road.

cards.front: What is the short version of recovering when you run off the pavement?
cards.back: The short version for running off the pavement is to slow down, regain control and then turn slowly back onto the road.

cards.front: How does a planned move onto a paved shoulder differ from recovering after drifting off the pavement?
cards.back: Leaving the road onto a paved shoulder is done at or near traffic speed before slowing, but drifting off the pavement by accident calls for slowing to twenty-five miles per hour or less before steering back.

decks.domain: Defensive driving: night driving, driving situations, emergencies, vehicle failures and crashes

cards.front: How do most car fires start, and what should you do if your car is on fire?
cards.back: Most car fires start with an electrical short circuit; get everyone out and away at once, call for help, and never try to fight the fire yourself.

cards.front: How long does a closed vehicle float in water, and what is the best way out?
cards.back: A vehicle with its windows and doors shut floats for about three to ten minutes, and the best escape is through an open window while it is still on the surface.

cards.front: How does the time a closed car floats compare with the time the manual calls plenty to get out?
cards.back: A car floating with its windows and doors closed stays up for about three to ten minutes, while the manual separately says three to five minutes is plenty of time to get out in an emergency.

cards.front: How does wearing a seat belt help if your vehicle goes into water?
cards.back: Wearing a seat belt improves your odds of surviving the impact with water and is the best protection against being knocked unconscious.

cards.front: When should you try power windows in water, and what can break side or rear glass?
cards.back: Try power windows immediately because they may short out, and side or rear glass can only be broken with a heavy, hard object.

cards.front: How does a front-engine vehicle sink, when does a door open more easily, and how do you find the surface?
cards.back: A front-engine vehicle sinks nose first, a door opens more easily once pressure inside and outside equalizes, and once outside you should follow the air bubbles to the surface.

cards.front: If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks, what must everyone do, and whom do you call?
cards.back: If the vehicle stalls on railroad tracks, everyone must get out and move far from the vehicle and tracks even when no train is coming, then call the number on the Emergency Notification sign or nine hundred eleven.

cards.front: If a train is approaching your stalled vehicle, which way should you run?
cards.back: If a train is approaching, run away from the vehicle and tracks at a forty-five-degree angle toward the direction the train is coming from, to avoid flying debris.

decks.domain: Defensive driving: night driving, driving situations, emergencies, vehicle failures and crashes

cards.front: If conventional disc and drum brakes fail, what should you do first?
cards.back: If conventional disc and drum brakes fail, downshift and then pump the pedal hard and quickly several times to try to build pressure.

cards.front: If pumping the brakes fails, how should you use the parking brake?
cards.back: If pumping fails, use the parking brake while holding its release so you can let up if the rear wheels lock and the vehicle starts to skid.

cards.front: How should you handle a flat tire or a blowout?
cards.back: With a flat or blowout, grip the wheel firmly, keep the vehicle straight, take your foot off the gas without braking, and coast to a stop in a safe spot.

cards.front: How does your foot work differ between failed conventional brakes and a tire blowout?
cards.back: When conventional brakes fail you pump the pedal, but during a tire blowout you take your foot off the gas and do not brake at all.

cards.front: What happens to the steering when the engine dies, and how do you get off the road?
cards.back: When the engine dies, power steering fails, so grip the wheel firmly and use extra force to steer the vehicle to a safe stop off the road.

cards.front: What should you do if the gas pedal sticks?
cards.back: If the gas pedal sticks, keep your eyes on the road, shift quickly to neutral, steer to a safe spot off the road, and turn off the engine.

cards.front: What should you do if the hood flies up while driving?
cards.back: If the hood flies up, slow down at once, look under the hood or out the side window, and use the center line or lane markings to guide the vehicle off the road.

cards.front: What should you do if your headlights suddenly go dark?
cards.back: If headlights suddenly go dark, stop safely off the road, try the headlight or dimmer switch, and if that fails switch on parking lights, flashers or turn signals and call for help.

cards.front: What should you do if the wipers quit during rain or snow?
cards.back: If the wipers quit during rain or snow, slow down, pull to a safe spot off the road and turn on the emergency flashers.

decks.domain: Defensive driving: night driving, driving situations, emergencies, vehicle failures and crashes

cards.front: When a collision threatens, what three choices do you have?
cards.back: When a collision threatens, the three choices are to stop, to turn or to speed up.

cards.front: To avoid a collision, how do you brake with antilock brakes, and how with conventional brakes?
cards.back: With antilock brakes, press as hard as needed and keep steering without pumping; with conventional brakes, pump them to keep steering control, since holding them down hard locks the wheels.

cards.front: How does braking to avoid a crash differ between ABS and conventional brakes?
cards.back: To avoid a crash with ABS you hold firm pressure without pumping, whereas with conventional brakes you pump to keep steering.

cards.front: When turning away from a crash, what should you avoid doing with the brakes?
cards.back: When turning away from a crash, avoid braking while you turn to lessen the chance of a skid, and do not brake hard when turning onto a soft shoulder.

cards.front: When is speeding up the right way to avoid a crash, and how do you do it?
cards.back: Speeding up is the right choice when you are about to be struck from the side or behind and there is open room ahead, so press the gas fully, then slow once clear.

cards.front: If a crash looks likely, which way should you steer, and what kind of object should you choose to hit?
cards.back: If a crash looks likely, steer away from oncoming traffic even if that means leaving the road, and choose to hit something that gives way, such as shrubs, rather than something hard.

cards.front: When something must be hit, how do you rank the choices, and what kind of blow do you aim for?
cards.back: When something must be hit, prefer an object moving your way over a stationary one, and a stationary one over one coming head-on, aiming for a glancing blow.

decks.module: Crash types and after a crash
decks.domain: Defensive driving: night driving, driving situations, emergencies, vehicle failures and crashes

cards.front: If you are about to be hit head-on while wearing a shoulder strap in a car with airbags, what should you do?
cards.back: If you are about to be hit head-on while wearing a shoulder strap in a car with airbags, protect your face with your arms and hands.

cards.front: In a head-on threat, how does your response differ with a shoulder strap and airbags versus without them?
cards.back: In a head-on threat with a shoulder strap and airbags you shield your face, but without a strap or airbags you throw yourself across the seat to avoid the wheel and windshield.

cards.front: If a rear-end crash is coming, how should you prepare?
cards.back: If a rear-end crash is coming, be ready to brake so you are not shoved into the car ahead, brace between the wheel and seat back and press your head against the headrest.

cards.front: If you are about to be hit from the side, what should you do?
cards.back: If you are about to be hit from the side, keep a tight grip on the wheel and be ready to turn quickly to regain control if the vehicle spins.

cards.front: Which crashes must New Jersey drivers report to police, and when may a body be moved?
cards.back: New Jersey requires drivers to notify police of any crash involving injury, death, or vehicle or property damage, and a body must not be moved until police or an ambulance arrive.

cards.front: What must you do after hitting a parked vehicle?
cards.back: After hitting a parked vehicle, you must notify the police and should also try to find the owner.

cards.front: What should you do at any crash you witness or are part of?
cards.back: At any crash you witness or are part of, stop, stay calm, get help from police and an ambulance, wait at the scene without blocking traffic and warn oncoming drivers.

cards.front: When must you send a written crash report to the MVC, by when, and whom else do you notify?
cards.back: When property damage exceeds five hundred dollars or someone is injured, send a written report to the MVC within ten days unless the police file one, and notify your insurer at once.

cards.front: When is no written MVC crash report needed, and what should you do if you are shaken up?
cards.back: No written MVC crash report is needed when the police file one, and you can get a copy of their report; if shaken up, see a doctor promptly.

recap_hooks.text: Most driving decisions rest on what you can see, and vision shrinks after dark, so slow down and keep your stop inside the reach of your headlights.
On low beams the night table grows fast: seventy-five feet in total at twenty, two hundred eleven at forty, four hundred nine at sixty and five hundred thirty at seventy.
Turn headlights on from dusk to dawn, on dark days and when weather limits sight to under five hundred feet, and in New Jersey any time the wipers run.
People on foot or in wheelchairs always own the crosswalk, marked or not, so be at your slowest by the time you reach it.
Keep your eyes twelve seconds or more down the road, which on a clear city street at twenty-five is about a block, and slow down in heavy traffic to buy reaction time.
Speed is a leading crash factor even on dry roads, so slow for warning signs and for animals, and treat an unsigned intersection as your job to handle.
Breaking the rules in a New Jersey construction zone costs double, and the warning can come up to half a mile before the work starts.
In a work zone, stay fully alert, follow signs and flaggers, keep headlights on and space ahead, and skip the radio and hands-free calls.
Expect a detour or a lane shift, and wait for the End Road Work sign or the last temporary device before driving normally again.
Lift off the gas and steer the way the rear is sliding, never sharply away and never on the brakes in a side skid, then straighten up once in control.
For a planned stop, get onto a paved shoulder near traffic speed, put one warning device just behind the car and another three hundred feet back.
If the wheels wander off the edge, stay there, ease off, and only turn a quarter turn back toward the road once at twenty-five miles per hour or less.
Car fires mostly start from an electrical short, so get everyone out and away and call for help instead of fighting it yourself.
A closed car floats for three to ten minutes, so buckle up, try the windows right away and get out through an open window while it is still on the surface.
Stalled on the tracks means everyone out and far away, and with a train coming, run away from the car and tracks at an angle toward the direction it is coming from.
Failed brakes call for a downshift and hard pumping, then the parking brake with its release held, while a blowout calls for a straight wheel and no brakes at all.
A stuck pedal means neutral, a safe spot and engine off, and a raised hood means slowing at once and following the lane markings off the road.
When lights or wipers quit, get safely off the road, and switch on flashers or other lights.
Facing a crash, you can stop, turn or speed up; with ABS press hard and steer, and with conventional brakes pump to keep steering.
Speed up only when a hit from the side or behind is coming and the road ahead is open, and do not brake while turning away.
If you must hit something, steer away from oncoming traffic, pick something soft, and aim for a glancing blow rather than a head-on one.

recaps.module: Crash types and after a crash

recap_hooks.text: Head-on with a shoulder strap and airbags, shield your face; with neither, throw yourself across the seat; for a rear hit, brace and press your head back.
Tell the police about every crash with injury, death or damage, including a parked car you hit, and never move a body before help arrives.
Send the MVC a written report within ten days when damage tops five hundred dollars or someone is hurt, unless the police already filed one.
